[[File:Cube graphs.svg|thumb|400px|The edge graphs of the [[square]], [[cube]] and [[tesseract]].]]

In [[polytopes|polytope theory]], the '''edge graph''' (also known as '''vertex-edge graph''' or just '''graph''') of a [[polytope]] is a combinatorial [[graph (graph theory)|graph]] whose vertices and edges correspond directly to the [[Vertex (geometry)|vertices]] and [[Edge (geometry)|edges]] of the polytope.
As a purely [[Combinatorics|combinatorial]] object, the edge graph encodes incidence information, capturing which vertices are connected by edges, but it does not retain geometric data such as vertex positions or edge lengths. 
Further common names for the edge graph are '''[[n-skeleton|skeleton]]''' and {{nowrap|'''1-skeleton'''}}, though some authors reserve these terms for the geometric embedding formed by the vertices and edges in the polytope's [[ambient space]].
There is no universally agreed upon notation for the edge graph of a polytope <math>P</math>. Common notations include <math>G_P</math>, <math>G(P)</math> or <math>\operatorname{skel}(P)</math>.

Not all graphs are realizable as edge graphs of polytopes; those that are realizable in this manner are called '''polytopal graphs'''.
Edge graphs of [[polyhedron|3-dimensional polytopes]] are also called [[polyhedral graph]]s. 
The problem of deciding whether a given graph is polytopal or not is known as the '''realization problem''' and is NP hard in general dimension.{{citation needed|date=July 2025}} In dimension three the problem is also called the '''Steinitz problem''' in recognition of its resolution by [[Ernst Steinitz]].

Information about the polytope's faces of dimension two or higher is not immediately accessible from the edge graph, and often cannot be reconstruction from it at all.
To capture the full combinatorial structure of a polytope, including the number of faces of each dimension and the incidence relations between them, one needs to work with the polytope's [[face lattice]].
In analogy to the term "1-skeleton", the part of the face lattice that contains the information about the combinatorics of faces up to dimension <math>k</math> is called the ''<math>k</math>-skeleton'' of the polytope.

== General properties ==

The edge graph of a [[convex polytope]] is a finite [[simple graph]]. 
It is [[Connected graph|connected]], since a path between any two vertices can be obtained from the [[simplex algorithm]].
For low-dimensional polytopes the structure of the edge graph is essentially determined by the polytope's dimension:

* the only 0-dimensional polytope is the point; its edge graph is <math>K_1</math>.
* the only 1-dimensional polytope is the line segment; its edge graph is <math>K_2</math>.
* the 2-dimensional polytopes are [[polygon]]s. The edge graph of an <math>n</math>-sided polygon is <math>C_n</math>, the [[cycle graph|cycle]] with <math>n</math> vertices.
* the edge graphs of 3-dimensional polytopes are rich in structure but well-understood: by [[Steinitz's theorem]] the edge graphs of 3-polytopes are precisely the [[vertex connectivity|3-vertex-connected]] [[planar graph]]s, for this reason also known as [[polyhedral graph]]s.

For <math>d</math>-polytopes with <math>d\ge 4</math> no characterization of edge graphs is known.
Some general statements can be made:

* the edge graph has [[Vertex degree|minimum degree]] at least <math>d</math>. If every vertex of a <math>d</math>-polytope has degree exactly <math>d</math> (i.e. the edge graph is [[regular graph|<math>d</math>-regular]]), then the polytope is said to be [[simple polytope|simple]].
* the edge graph is [[vertex connectivity|<math>d</math>-vertex connected]]. This is known as [[Balinski's theorem]].
* the edge graph contains a [[topological minor|subdivision]] of the [[complete graph]] <math>K_{d+1}</math>.<ref name="Grünbaum"/> In particular, for <math>d\ge 4</math>, the edge graph contains a <math>K_5</math>-minor and is not planar.

It is in general non-trivial to determine whether a given graph is the edge graph of a polytope, that is, whether it is a ''polytopal graph''. For some graph classes, such as graphs of minimum degree <math>\delta\le 3</math>, the above properties can help to decide this question. 
For example, the [[Petersen graph]] is [[regular graph|3-regular]]. Hence, if it were polytopal, it would be the edge graph of a 3-dimensional polytope. 
The Petersen graph is however not planar and thus cannot be the edge graph of a 3-polytope.

For graphs of minimum degree <math>\delta\ge 4</math> such questions are generally much harder to answer.
For example, as of July 2025 it is unknown whether the [[Cartesian product of graphs|Cartesian graph product]] of two Petersen graphs is polytopal.<ref>https://www.math.uni-bielefeld.de/geocomb/assets/Slides_Ziegler.pdf, Section 7</ref> It is known that if it were polytopal, then the polytope must be of dimension four or five.<ref name="Pfeifle"/>

== Examples ==

=== Named families ===

* The [[cycle graph]] <math>C_n</math> is the edge graph of the <math>n</math>-sided [[polygon]].
* The [[complete graph]] <math>K_n</math> is the edge graph of the <math>(n-1)</math>-dimensional [[simplex]] (including the [[triangle]], [[tetrahedron]] and [[5-cell]]). 
* The [[hypercube graph]] <math>Q_n</math> is th edge graph of the <math>n</math>-dimensional [[hypercube]] (including [[square]] and [[cube]]). Its distance-two graph is known as the [[halved cube graph]] and is the edge graphs of the corresponding [[demihypercube]].
* The [[Turán graph]] <math>T(2n,n)</math> (also known as "cocktail party graph" <ref>{{cite web | title=Cocktail Party Graph | url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/CocktailPartyGraph.html }}</ref>) is the edge graph of the <math>n</math>-dimensional [[cross-polytope]] (including [[octahedron]] and [[16-cell]]).
* The [[Johnson graph]] <math>J(n,k)</math> is the edge graph of the [[hypersimplex]] <math>\Delta_{n,k}</math>.
* The [[Hamming graph]] <math>H(d,q)</math> is the edge graph of the <math>d</math>-th [[Cartesian product|cartesian power]] of the <math>(q-1)</math>-dimensional simplex. This includes the edge graphs of both simplices <math>H(1,q)</math> and hypercubes <math>H(d,2)</math>, but also other polytopes such as the [[3-3 duoprism|(3,3)-duoprism]] <math>H(2,3)</math>.
* The [[Bruhat graph]] is the edge graph of the [[permutahedron]]. More generally, the [[Cayley graph]] of a finite [[Coxeter group]] (with the natural generators) is the edge graph of the corresponding [[Omnitruncation|omnitruncated]] [[uniform polytope]], or more generally, the edge graph of a generic [[orbit polytope]] of the associated [[reflection group]].

=== Other named examples ===

* The [[icosahedral graph]] is the edge graph of the [[regular icosahedron]].
* The [[dodecahedral graph]] is the edge graph of the [[regular dodecahedron]].
* The [[Schläfli graph]] is the edge graph of the 6-dimensional [[2 21 polytope|2<sub>21</sub> polytope]].
* The [[Gosset graph]] is the edge graph of the 7-dimensional [[3 21 polytope|3<sub>21</sub> polytope]].

== Operations ==

Some operations on polytopes translate to their edge graphs in a natural way.

* The edge graph of the [[Cartesian product]] <math>P\times Q</math> of two polytopes is the [[Cartesian product of graphs|Cartesian graph product]] of the edge graphs of <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math>. For example, the product of a cycle graph and <math>K_1</math> is the edge graph of a [[Prism (geometry)|prism]]. There are non-polytopal graphs whose product is polytopal.<ref name="Pfeifle"/>
* The edge graph of the [[join (topology)|join]] <math>P\star Q</math> of two polytopes is the [[Graph operations#Binary operations|graph join]] of the edge graphs of <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math>. The graph join is constructed from the disjoint union of the edge graphs by adding all edges between them. The same edge graph is obtained for the [[Direct sum of polytopes|direct sum]] <math>P\oplus Q</math> (the dual of the Cartesian product) under the assumption that both <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> are of dimension at least two.
* For 3-dimensional polytopes the edge graph of the [[dual polytope]] is the [[dual graph]] of its edge graph.

== Reconstruction from the edge graph ==

Given the edge graph of a polytope of dimension three or lower it is possible to reconstruct the polytope's [[face lattice|full combinatorics]], that is, the complete list of faces and incidences between them.
For example, the 2-dimensional faces of a 3-polytope correspond exactly to the [[Vertex separator|non-separating]] [[induced subgraph|induced]] [[cycle graph|cycles]] in the edge graph.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Diestel |first=Reinhard |date=2025 |title=Graph Theory |url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-662-70107-2 |journal=Graduate Texts in Mathematics |volume=173 |language=en |pages= |doi=10.1007/978-3-662-70107-2 |isbn=978-3-662-70106-5 |issn=0072-5285|url-access=subscription }} Proposition 4.2.7</ref>
Also, for polytopes of dimension up to three it is possible to tell the dimension of the polytope from the edge graph.
In dimension <math>d\ge 4</math> neither of this is the case. There exist combinatorially distinct polytopes with [[graph isomorphism|isomorphic]] edge graphs, and even polytopes of different dimensions with isomorphic edge graphs.

=== Examples of non-reconstructability ===

The edge graph of a [[simplex]] is a [[complete graph]].
However, in dimension <math>d\ge 4</math> there are other polytopes whose edge graph is complete. 
These are called [[neighborly polytope|1-neighborly polytopes]]. 
For example, both the <math>d</math>-dimension simplex and the 4-dimensional [[cyclic polytope]] <math>C_4(d+1)</math> have edge graph <math>K_{d+1}</math>.

[[Hypercubes]] of sufficiently large dimension share their edge graphs with ''neighborly cubical polytopes''. For example, the edge graph of the 10-dimensional hypercube is also the edge graph of a 4-dimensional polytope.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Joswig |first1=M. |last2=Ziegler |first2=G. M. |date=2000-09-01 |title=Neighborly Cubical Polytopes |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s004540010039 |journal=Discrete & Computational Geometry |language=en |volume=24 |issue=2 |pages=325–344 |doi=10.1007/s004540010039 |issn=1432-0444|arxiv=math/9812033 }}</ref>

One general technique for obtaining combinatorially distinct polytopes with the same edge graph is by constructing both the [[Direct sum of polytopes|direct sum]] and the [[join (topology)|join]] of two polytopes.
While these operations never generate polytopes of the same dimension, the resulting polytopes always have the same edge graph (assuming that we start from polytopes of dimension at least two).
For example, the join <math>\Delta\star \Delta</math> of two triangles is a 5-dimensional simplex, whereas the direct sum <math>\Delta\oplus\Delta</math> is the 4-dimensional cyclic polytope on six vertices <math>C_4(6)</math>. Both have <math>K_6</math> as their edge graph.

=== Reconstruction in special cases ===

Reconstruction of the polytope's [[face lattice|full combinatorics]] from the edge graph is possible in special cases or when additional data is available:

<!--{{unsolved|mathematics|Is the combinatorial type determined by the edge graph and edge lengths?}}-->
* The combinatorics of a [[simple polytope]] can be reconstructed from the edge graph. This was first proven by Blind & Mani.<ref name="BlindMani"/> Later, a short proof was given by [[Gil Kalai]] using [[unique sink orientation]]s.<ref name="Kalai" />
* The combinatorics of a [[zonotope]] can be reconstructed from the edge graph.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Björner |first1=Anders |last2=Edelman |first2=Paul H. |last3=Ziegler |first3=Günter M. |date=1990-06-01 |title=Hyperplane arrangements with a lattice of regions |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02187790 |journal=Discrete & Computational Geometry |language=en |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=263–288 |doi=10.1007/BF02187790 |issn=1432-0444}} Theorem 6.14</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Babson |first1=Eric |last2=Finschi |first2=Lukas |last3=Fukuda |first3=Komei |date=2001-07-01 |title=Cocircuit Graphs and Efficient Orientation Reconstruction in Oriented Matroids |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1006/eujc.2001.0481 |journal=Eur. J. Comb. |volume=22 |issue=5 |pages=587–600 |doi=10.1006/eujc.2001.0481 |issn=0195-6698|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* For simplicial polytopes, given the polytope's edge graph and its [[Geometric rigidity|space of self-stresses]] it is possible to reconstruct the polytope up to affine equivalence.<ref name="NovikZheng"/>

== Other relations ==

* The [[simplex algorithm]] traverses the edge graph of a polytope to find the optimal solution to a [[linear program]].
<!--* Edge graphs of d-polytopes have minimum degree at least d. By [[Balinski's theorem]] edge graphs of d-polytopes are even [[d-vertex connected]]. Even stronger, they contain a subdivision of <math>K_{d+1}</math>. Conversely, it is not true that the edge graph of a <math>d</math>-polytope is <math>K_{d+2}</math>-free, except for <math>d\le 3</math>. For <math>d=3</math> edge graphs are planar and hence free of <math>K_5</math>.-->
* The [[Hirsch conjecture]] asserts that the edge graph of a <math>d</math>-polytope has [[diameter (graph theory)|diameter]] at most <math>d</math>. A counterexample was found by Santos in 2012,.<ref name="Santos"/> The conjecture has since been reformulated in different ways. As of June 2025, no polynomial bound on the diameter in <math>d</math> is known.
* Historically, the terms "vertex" and "edge" for graphs originated in the study of [[polyhedron|polyhedra]] and were only subsequently adopted into [[graph theory]].
